sermon:
## The Mission You Cannot Start
*Why the risen Lord tells his church to wait*

**Text:** Acts 1:1-26 · **Supporting:** Luke 24:49; John 16:7; Acts 2:33; Zechariah 4:6

The church begins with men told to do nothing. Forty days of resurrection appearances, the empty tomb behind them, the King alive in front of them, and the first command is not go. It is wait. We have built a whole religion of activity on a foundation that opens with a closed door.

**The Author Who Has Not Stopped Writing**
Luke addresses his second volume to Theophilus and tells him plainly what the first one was: "In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach" (Acts 1:1). Began. The Gospel of Luke was not the whole life of Christ. It was the beginning of it. Everything that follows in Acts — the sermons, the prisons, the shipwreck, the open door at Rome — is what Jesus continues to do, now from the throne, through the Spirit, in the church. The ascension is not the end of his ministry. It is the relocation of it. He did not retire to heaven. He took a seat there. "He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God" (Acts 1:3). The risen Christ teaches for forty days and the subject is the kingdom — not their plans, not their timetable, not their organizational chart, but his reign. Then a cloud takes him out of their sight, and two men in white ask them why they stand gazing into heaven. The point of the ascension is not that he is gone. It is that he is enthroned, and the work goes on under a King who is now seated above it. Whatever the church does from here, it does as the continued work of a living Lord, not the memorial society of a dead teacher.

**The Question He Will Not Answer**
They ask the question we would all ask. "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). They want the schedule. They want the map. They want to know how soon the thing they have been hoping for finally arrives, and on whose timetable. And he refuses to give it. "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority" (Acts 1:7). The Father has fixed them. They are real, they are appointed, and they are none of your business. Then he hands them something better than information. "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8). Not a date. A power. Not a strategy. A Spirit. Not a calendar of the end, but a commission for the middle. Zechariah said it to a discouraged people centuries before, to men trying to rebuild a temple with their own diminished strength: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). The mission has always run on this fuel and no other. Jesus had already told them in the upper room, on the night he was betrayed, "It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you" (John 16:7). His leaving is their gain, because his leaving sends the Spirit, and the Spirit is the engine of everything Acts records. They wanted the King to stay and finish it himself. He tells them his absence is the condition of their power.

**The Waiting We Refuse**
Here is where I have to put myself in the room with the eleven, because I have been the man who would not wait. I have launched the program and called it faith. I have mistaken motion for obedience, filled the silence with my own competence, treated the work of God like a thing I could manufacture if I just tried harder and stayed later and planned tighter. The command in Luke's parallel is plain: "stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high" (Luke 24:49). Stay. Be clothed. Receive. The verbs are passive on purpose. The church does not generate the Spirit; it waits to be filled by him. And what do the disciples do while they wait? They are not idle. They devote themselves to prayer, and they put the house in order — Peter leads them to replace Judas from among the men who had been with them from the baptism of John to the day of the ascension, and they pray, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen" (Acts 1:24), and they cast lots, and Matthias is numbered with the eleven. That is what waiting on God actually looks like. Not paralysis, but readiness without control. They do the ordinary, faithful, unglamorous work of getting ready, and they leave the outcome to the Lord who knows all hearts. Pentecost is coming, but they do not know the day. They only know the promise. And so they wait inside it.

We want the kingdom restored on our calendar. He gives us the Spirit on his. We want to know the times and the seasons. He gives us power to be witnesses where we already stand. The whole book of Acts is the difference between those two things, and the church that confuses them dies of exhaustion doing work God never asked it to begin. The risen Christ is building his church, and he builds it by his Spirit, in his time, through witnesses who learned first how to wait. The mission was begun by him in the Gospel, and it is carried by him through the book of Acts, and the most spiritual thing the early church ever did was sit still in an upper room until heaven moved. If your hands are full of work he never gave you, the problem is not that you are lazy. The problem is that you would not wait.

Wait. The mission is his.

## The Lord You Killed Now Reigns
*Pentecost and the only fit answer to the resurrection*

**Text:** Acts 2:1-41 · **Supporting:** Joel 2:28-32; Psalm 16:10; Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:33

The Spirit comes with the sound of a violent wind and the church is born in the middle of an accusation. Three thousand people will be saved that day, and they will be saved by being told they are murderers. We have made Pentecost a celebration of power. Peter made it a courtroom.

**The Promise Poured Out**
What the crowd sees first looks like chaos — Galileans speaking the languages of every nation under heaven, Parthians and Medes and Elamites hearing the mighty works of God each in his own tongue. The amazement splits two ways. Some are bewildered and ask what it means; the cynics in the crowd reach for the easy explanation: "They are filled with new wine" (Acts 2:13). Peter stands with the eleven and does not deny the strangeness. He explains it from the prophets. "This is what was uttered through the prophet Joel: 'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy'" (Acts 2:16-17). Joel had promised it generations earlier — the Spirit no longer rationed to a few kings and prophets but poured out on all flesh, on the old and the young, the servant and the free (Joel 2:28-29). And Joel had said something else Peter does not skip: "Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved" (Acts 2:21). The last days have begun. Not because the world ended, but because the Spirit came. Pentecost is the proof that the age of promise is over and the age of fulfillment has arrived. And the engine of it all — the wind, the fire, the tongues, the whole new age — is a man who was dead three days before. Peter will spend the rest of the sermon making sure they understand that this is not a wonder to gape at. It is a verdict to answer.

**The Sermon That Convicts**
Peter's message is one long argument with one inescapable conclusion. "Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:22-23). Two things at once, and Peter will not soften either. God planned the cross. You committed it. The sovereignty of God does not erase the guilt of the men who drove the nails; it stands over it without excusing it. And then the turn the whole sermon was built toward: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it" (Acts 2:24). Not possible. Death tried to hold him and could not, because he is who he is. Peter proves it from David. "You will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). David died and his tomb is with us to this day, Peter says — so David was not speaking of himself. He was speaking of his greater Son, the descendant God swore would sit on his throne. And then Psalm 110, the verse Jesus himself once pressed on the Pharisees until they could not answer: "The Lord said to my Lord, 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool'" (Psalm 110:1). The crucified Galilean is now the enthroned Lord. "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing" (Acts 2:33). The wind and the fire are not the headline. They are the receipt. Christ is on the throne and the proof of it is the very thing ringing in your ears right now.

**Cut to the Heart**
Here is the verdict that undoes the crowd: "Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified" (Acts 2:36). The Lord you killed now reigns. The man you handed to Pilate sits at the right hand of God. And I need to say plainly that this is not a sermon about people long dead in a city far away. It is a sermon about us, because the same sin that nailed him is the sin I excuse on a Tuesday — the preference for myself over God, the management of my own little kingdom, the quiet murder of the One who gets in my way and dares to claim the throne I want for myself. I did not stand in Pilate's courtyard. I have stood in my own and chosen Barabbas a hundred times. "Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, 'Brothers, what shall we do?'" (Acts 2:37). That is the only honest response to the resurrection. Not admiration. Not historical interest. Not a polite nod at an inspiring story. A wound. The risen Christ, building his church by the Spirit he has just poured out, does his very first work by breaking the people he intends to save, opening their hearts the way a plow opens hard ground. Peter answers, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself" (Acts 2:38-39). The hands that killed him are washed clean by the blood they spilled. Three thousand were added that day — not because the preacher was clever, but because the Lord they had crucified was now alive and reigning, and the Spirit gave them eyes to see it.

The Lord you killed now reigns.

## In the Name He Walks
*The power that betrays who has been with Jesus*

**Text:** Acts 3:1-4:31 · **Supporting:** Acts 4:12; Acts 3:6; Acts 4:13; Acts 4:20

A beggar sits at a gate called Beautiful and has sat there long enough that everyone steps around him without seeing him. He is the furniture of the temple, a fixture of the religious economy, asking for coins from people on their way to pray. He has been carried to that gate every day for years. Then two men with no money stop and look at him, and the whole city has to reckon with a name.

**The Name That Has the Power**
Peter says the line that exposes the entire early church. "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk" (Acts 3:6). No silver, no gold, no apparatus, no institution, no budget, no platform. A name. And the man who never walked, whose ankles had never borne his weight, leaps up and goes into the temple walking and leaping and praising God, and the people who had stepped around him for years are filled with wonder and amazement. They run together at Solomon's portico to gawk. Peter catches the misreading before it can harden into a cult of the apostles. "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?" (Acts 3:12). Not our power. Not our piety. The name. "And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know" (Acts 3:16). The same Jesus who healed the lame in the flesh in Galilee now heals the lame through his name from the throne, because he is not dead and gone, not a memory the apostles are keeping alive by force of will. He is alive and working, and the proof of it is dancing in the temple courts. The sign is a sermon: the power Jesus carried in his hands he carries still, and he carries it through ordinary men who have nothing to offer but his name.

**The Boldness That Betrays Them**
The healing lands Peter and John in front of the council — the same council that condemned Jesus a few weeks before, the rulers and elders and scribes, Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and all the high-priestly family, the men with all the silver and gold and power and piety in Jerusalem. And here are two fishermen, arrested overnight, hauled up to answer for a miracle. Luke records what the council cannot get past. "Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus" (Acts 4:13). That last line is the whole diagnosis of the early church. The council cannot account for the boldness. The men have no training, no credentials, no rabbinic pedigree, no standing in the room. What they have is a history — they had been with Jesus, and you cannot be with the risen Christ and stay timid. Peter does not flinch in front of the men who could ruin him, the very men who arranged the death of his Lord. He preaches the cross to their faces. "Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well" (Acts 4:10). And then the verse that has scandalized every pluralist since: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). One name. No other. The council does not want this. Neither does our age, which has built a religion of many doors. And neither, if I am honest, do I always want a gospel that leaves the cultured no exit, because it offends the same instinct in me that wants to keep my respectability and my Christ at the same time, to be liked by the people who hate the exclusivity of his name.

**We Cannot Be Quiet**
The council does the only thing power can do when it has run out of argument — it threatens. They confer privately, admit they cannot deny the miracle the whole city saw, and decide to manage it by intimidation. "They called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus" (Acts 4:18). And here is the answer the persecuted church has thrown back at every tyrant since: "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:19-20). We cannot stop. Not we will not — we cannot. The church here is not brave by willpower; it is full of something it cannot contain, a witness pressing to get out. And when they are released and return to their friends, they do not regroup to strategize their safety. They pray — and not for protection, but for more boldness, asking God to look on the threats and grant his servants to speak the word with all confidence while he stretches out his hand to heal in the name of his holy servant Jesus. "And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness" (Acts 4:31). The risen Christ builds his church by filling common men with his Spirit and his name, until silence becomes a thing they are no longer capable of. I have been quiet where they could not be. I have edited the offensive name out of the conversation to keep the peace, kept my mouth shut to keep my comfort. The difference between Peter and me is not courage. The difference is how recently I have been with him.

We cannot stop speaking him.

## God Is Not Your Audience
*The lie the Spirit will not be performed for*

**Text:** Acts 4:32-6:7 · **Supporting:** Acts 5:4; Acts 5:3; Acts 6:2; Acts 6:4

Luke shows us a church so unified it shares everything, and then in the same breath shows us two people struck dead for a donation. We want the first picture. We skip the second. But Luke set them side by side on purpose, because the same Spirit who makes the church generous is the Spirit who will not be lied to, and the church that forgets the second loses the first.

**The Body That Shares Itself**
The portrait is almost unbelievable. "Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common" (Acts 4:32). This is not legislated communism; it is grace overflowing its banks. There was not a needy person among them, because those who owned lands or houses sold them and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. The grace was so heavy on them that ownership simply loosened its grip. Luke names a model so we cannot miss the texture of it — a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, son of encouragement, who sold a field and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet. Generosity with no audience, no announcement, just a man who counted his property less than his brothers. And then, against that bright backdrop, two figures step out of the same congregation and do the same outward act for the opposite reason.

**The Managed Lie**
Ananias, with his wife Sapphira's knowledge, sells a piece of property and keeps back part of the price for himself, and brings the rest and lays it at the apostles' feet as though it were the whole. The sin is not that they kept some back. Peter makes that explicit, and it matters enormously that he does. "While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?" (Acts 5:4). They were free to give part. They were free to give nothing at all. No one demanded the field, no one set a quota. The sin was the performance — the staged generosity, the curated appearance of a wholehearted devotion they did not actually have, the buying of a reputation for sacrifice on the cheap. Peter names the real defendant behind it. "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land?" (Acts 5:3). And then the line that should empty every one of us of our religious theater: "You have not lied to men but to God" (Acts 5:4). They thought their audience was the apostles, the watching church, the brothers who would admire the gift and tell the story. Their audience was God. Ananias fell down and breathed his last, and great fear came on all who heard. Three hours later his wife came in, not knowing, and Peter gave her the chance to tell the truth, and she told the same lie, and she fell at his feet and died, "and great fear came upon the whole church" (Acts 5:11). We flinch at the severity. We should flinch harder at the lie, because I have stood in a pulpit and performed a holiness I did not possess, played to a room while my heart was somewhere else, and the only reason I am still standing is mercy, not innocence. The Spirit who fills the body will not be managed, will not be impressed, will not be played to. He is not seated in the audience grading the performance. He is on the throne, and he sees the kept-back part.

**The Word and the Tables**
The second test is gentler but no less revealing about where the church's life is hidden. The church grows, and a complaint arises among the believers — the Hellenist widows, the Greek-speaking ones, are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. A real need, a real injustice, the kind of thing that quietly fractures a body. And the apostles could have absorbed it. They could have made themselves indispensable to every department, the men without whom nothing functioned. Instead they refuse the wrong work, plainly. "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables" (Acts 6:2). Not because tables do not matter — they appoint seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to that very service, and the Spirit honors the work of tables so highly that one of those seven is Stephen, who becomes the first martyr, and another is Philip, who carries the gospel to Samaria and the Ethiopian. The work of waiting on widows produces a martyr and an evangelist. The apostles refuse the table-work because their own calling is narrower and they know it and they will guard it. "But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4). Here is the discipline I most often fail: the willingness to do my one thing and not everything, to let other Spirit-filled people carry what God did not give me to carry, to refuse the good work that would slowly bury the word under busyness and call the burying servanthood. And Luke gives the result like a verdict that ties the whole passage together: "And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith" (Acts 6:7). The church that will not lie to God and will not let the word be crowded out by good things is the church the risen Christ builds by his Spirit. He sees the staged gift in the dark. He is the audience of every hidden motive. And he is not impressed by the show you put on for the people in the room.

God is not your audience.

## The Witness Dies Still Seeing
*Stephen, and a face that looked like an angel*

**Text:** Acts 6:8-7:60 · **Supporting:** Acts 7:51; Acts 7:56; Acts 7:60; Acts 7:55

The first man to die for the name of Jesus dies in the middle of a Bible study. Stephen is seized, dragged before the council on false witnesses, charged with speaking against the temple and the law — and the council looks at him and sees that his face is like the face of an angel. What he gives them is not a defense. It is the whole history of Israel read as a single, terrible pattern, and at the end of it, they kill him for telling the truth about themselves.

**The History That Indicts**
The high priest asks if the charges are true, and Stephen answers by walking them through their own Scriptures — Abraham called out of Mesopotamia, the promise made before there was a son to fulfill it, Joseph, Moses, the wilderness, the tabernacle, the temple. He is not stalling, and he is not showing off his learning. He is reading their history honestly, and in the telling a pattern surfaces that they cannot bear to see. Again and again God sends a deliverer, and again and again the people reject him before they receive him. Joseph, sold by his own brothers out of jealousy, becomes the very man God uses to save them from famine. Moses, refused at first by the man he tried to help — "Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?" — becomes their rescuer at the burning bush. And when Moses brings them out, the fathers would not obey him "but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt" (Acts 7:39), making a golden calf at the very foot of the mountain. Stephen is not insulting their history. He is reading it the way it actually reads. And honest history has a verdict. "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you" (Acts 7:51). The pattern did not stop with the prophets. It climaxed in the Righteous One. "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered" (Acts 7:52). The men who guard the temple are not the exception to the story; they are the latest link in a chain of resistance that runs the whole length of the nation. The mirror is unbearable, and they reach for stones rather than look into it. They are enraged, and they grind their teeth at him, because the truth about ourselves is the one charge we will kill to avoid.

**The Heaven That Opens**
What happens next is the heart of the whole scene, and it is the comfort the church has carried into every prison and every arena since. Stephen, accused, surrounded, with the fury rising and death already in the air, does not look at his accusers. "But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God" (Acts 7:55). And he says it out loud, into the teeth of the men holding the stones: "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God" (Acts 7:56). Notice the posture, because Luke chose the word with care. Elsewhere the risen Christ is seated, reigning, the work finished, the enemies being made his footstool. Here he is standing — risen from the throne to receive his dying witness, on his feet for the man who will not deny him under the stones. The first martyr of the church does not die abandoned in the dust outside the city. He dies seeing the very Lord he is dying for, and the Lord is not distant, not indifferent, not waiting passively in glory. He is standing. The heavens are not closed over the head of the one who suffers for the name. They open. And the Son of Man, the very title Jesus used of himself before this same council at his own trial, is on his feet for his people at the cost. Whatever it costs to follow him, it does not cost the sight of him.

**The Prayer That Echoes the Cross**
And then Stephen does the thing that proves beyond argument whose Spirit fills him. They drag him out of the city, the witnesses lay their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul, and they stone him. And as the stones come down on him, he prays the prayer his Lord prayed first. "And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.'" And then, falling to his knees under the blows, "he cried out with a loud voice, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.' And when he had said this, he fell asleep" (Acts 7:59-60). Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do, Jesus said from the cross — and now his witness says it under the stones, with the same breath, in the same Spirit, to the same God. This is what it looks like when the Spirit fills a man all the way to the end. Not clenched, not cursing, not bargaining for one more hour. Forgiving his killers and seeing his Lord, and Luke softens the horror with one word — he fell asleep. I have to be honest that I do not know if I have this in me, because I nurse grievances far smaller than my own murder and call the grudge righteousness, rehearse the wrongs done to me and call the rehearsal justice. Stephen had none of it. And Luke quietly tells us that the young man Saul was standing there, holding the coats, approving of the execution — and the Lord who stood for Stephen was already at work on the man who would take Stephen's place as the great witness to the nations. The risen Christ builds his church on the blood of people who die still seeing him, and the seeing is the mercy that holds them through the stones.

The witness dies still seeing.

## Scattered, and Still Preaching
*How persecution became the engine of the mission*

**Text:** Acts 8:1-40 · **Supporting:** Acts 8:4; Acts 1:8; Acts 8:35; Acts 8:39

The enemy of the church looks at Stephen's body in the dust and decides to finish the job. A great persecution breaks out, Saul ravages the church house to house and drags men and women off to prison, and the believers are driven out of Jerusalem in every direction. From where Saul stands it looks like victory. It is the worst day the young church has seen. It is also the day the gospel left the city.

**The Scattering That Spreads**
Luke records the disaster in one verse and the result in the next, and the contrast between them is the whole sermon. "And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles" (Acts 8:1). Scattered — and in the Greek it is the word a farmer uses for sowing seed. The persecutor thinks he is stamping out a fire. He is broadcasting it across a field. And then the verse that turns the disaster inside out: "Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word" (Acts 8:4). Not the apostles, who stayed in Jerusalem. Not the appointed leaders or the trained teachers. The ordinary, nameless, scattered believers, running for their lives with their households on their backs, went about preaching wherever the scattering threw them. The persecution meant to silence the church became the means of spreading it. Remember what the risen Christ said before he ascended: "You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8). They had stayed in Jerusalem. They were comfortable in Jerusalem, gathered, growing, safe in their numbers. It took a persecution to push them out into Judea and Samaria — to make them do the thing he had told them to do. God did not author the sin of the men who hunted his people. He governed it. He took the worst thing the enemy could do and used it to launch the mission the church had been too settled to begin on its own. So I should be slow to read my own scatterings only as defeat, because the providence that runs through this chapter has not retired, and the field it sows is sometimes my own upended life.

**The Wall That Falls**
Where does the gospel go first when it leaves Jerusalem? Straight to Samaria — to the half-breeds, the heretics, the people a good Jew crossed the road to avoid, the old enemy on the northern border. Philip, one of the seven appointed to wait on tables, goes down to a city of Samaria and proclaims Christ there, and the crowds with one accord pay attention, and there is much joy in that city. The first wall is down. The gospel that began among Jerusalem Jews crosses into the very people Jerusalem despised, because the risen Christ is no respecter of the boundaries we guard so carefully and call holy. And then God pushes it further still, out of the city and onto a lonely road. An angel sends Philip south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza, and there is a chariot, and in it an Ethiopian eunuch — a foreigner, a court official of the queen of the Ethiopians, a man whose mutilated body had barred him from the assembly under the old law — returning home, reading the prophet Isaiah aloud and not understanding it. The Spirit tells Philip to go and join the chariot, and Philip runs to it and hears the man reading and asks, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And the eunuch answers, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" (Acts 8:31). He is reading the very heart of it: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth" (Acts 8:32). He asks Philip of whom the prophet speaks, himself or someone else. "Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus" (Acts 8:35). The whole gospel, drawn straight out of the suffering servant — the lamb led to slaughter who is the crucified and risen Lord. They come to some water, and the eunuch says, "See, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?" (Acts 8:36). The law had once prevented him. Christ had removed the wall. Nothing prevents him now.

**The Joy That Goes Home**
And then a strange, glad ending that tells you who the chapter has been about all along. "And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing" (Acts 8:39). The preacher vanishes and the convert rejoices. Philip was never the point; he is the instrument the Spirit picks up, sets down, and reassigns. The eunuch goes home — to Africa, to the far southern edge of the known world, carrying the gospel further than any apostle had yet gone, a man the old covenant kept outside the door now baptized and rejoicing and homeward bound with the good news. This is how the whole mission moves. Not by a master plan the church drew up and executed in its own strength, but by a sovereign Spirit working through scattered, frightened, obedient people, tearing down the very walls they would have spent their lives defending. I have wanted the comfortable Jerusalem, the gathered safety, the church that stays put and grows quietly behind its own walls. God keeps scattering his church to the Samarias and the desert roads, because the risen Christ intends his name to reach the end of the earth, and he is not waiting on my comfort to do it. The thing the persecutor meant for the death of the church turned out to be the beginning of its reach.

Scattering is how it spreads.

## Why Do You Persecute Me
*Grace seizes the man hunting it*

**Text:** Acts 9:1-31 · **Supporting:** Acts 9:4; Acts 9:5; Acts 9:15; Acts 9:16

The worst enemy the church has does not drift toward faith over years of softening. He is stopped cold on a road, at the height of his rage, with arrest warrants in his hand and murder in his plans. Saul does not seek Christ. Christ seizes Saul. And that, in the end, is the only reason any of us are here at all.

**The Enemy on the Road**
Luke will not let us soften who this man is, because the whole point depends on it. "But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem" (Acts 9:1-2). Still breathing threats and murder. This is not a sincere seeker with a few honest doubts and a heart already half-turned. This is a man whose every exhale is violence, traveling a hundred and fifty miles to another city for the express purpose of dragging Christians home in chains — men and women, Luke specifies, husbands and wives and mothers. There is no spark of openness here to fan into flame. There is only fury with a legal warrant. And on that road, in the bright middle of that murderous errand, a light from heaven flashes around him and he falls to the ground and hears a voice. "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" (Acts 9:4). Not why are you persecuting my people. Not why are you persecuting my church. Me. Saul thought he was hunting a deluded sect, a movement built around a dead and discredited teacher. He was hunting the risen Christ himself, because the head feels every blow aimed at the body, and there is no wound you can deal the least of his that does not land on him. "Who are you, Lord?" Saul asks from the dust, and the answer reorganizes his entire universe in one sentence: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting" (Acts 9:5). The dead man Saul was certain was a fraud is alive, and speaking, and standing over him in a glory that strikes him blind. Everything Saul built his life on — his pedigree, his zeal, his certainty, his clean conscience — collapses in a breath. He is led by the hand into the city he came to terrorize, blind and fasting, waiting.

**The Vessel Chosen**
Now watch the sovereignty of it, because this is grace at its most offensive — offensive, that is, to anyone who quietly believes grace ought to go to the people who deserve it. The Lord appears in a vision to a disciple in Damascus named Ananias and sends him to lay hands on the blind persecutor. And Ananias objects, reasonably, the way any of us would: "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name" (Acts 9:13-14). Everyone knows who Saul is. His reputation arrived in Damascus before he did. And the Lord overrides the objection with a purpose Ananias could never have guessed in a hundred years. "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel" (Acts 9:15). Chosen. The man breathing murder this morning is the man God selected before the foundation of the world to carry his name to the ends of the earth. Not chosen because of anything God found in Saul — there is nothing in Saul but rage and résumé, a zeal aimed at the very throne of heaven. Chosen by sheer grace, while he was still an enemy with the warrants still warm in his bag. And then the Lord adds the cost, immediately, in the same breath as the calling: "For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name" (Acts 9:16). The man who made others suffer for the name will now suffer for it himself. The persecutor becomes the persecuted. This is what conversion to the risen Christ actually does — it does not merely pardon the enemy and send him on his way; it commissions him, and it commissions him to the very sufferings he once inflicted on others.

**The Grace That Has No Floor**
I have to sit down inside this one, because the easy lie of the religious life — the lie I tell myself in my best moments — is that I came to Christ because I was, deep down, the kind of person who would. The decent seeker. The honest doubter. The one with the soft heart God could work with. Saul ruins that lie completely. He was not the kind of person who would; he was the kind of person who would have arrested me and called it service to God. And grace took him anyway — not at his best, at his worst; not reaching out with an open hand, but with his fist still raised. "And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, 'He is the Son of God.' And all who heard him were amazed and said, 'Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name?'" (Acts 9:20-21). The synagogues that braced for an inquisitor got a preacher instead. The church that rightly feared him learned, slowly and through Barnabas who vouched for the man no one would believe, to receive him as a brother. And here is the comfort that should level every one of us: if grace can take Saul, grace has no floor beneath which a person is too far gone, no enemy too fierce, no record too red. The fiercest enemy the gospel ever had became its greatest witness, and he did nothing to earn it but lie in the road and get knocked down by a mercy he was not looking for and did not want. The risen Christ builds his church by seizing the very people most determined to tear it down. I did not climb up to him by the merit of my better instincts. He came down the road and took me where I lay. So did Saul. So, in the end, does every single person who is ever saved.

Grace seizes its worst enemy.

## God Has No Second Class
*The wall between us, torn down from heaven*

**Text:** Acts 10:1-11:18 · **Supporting:** Acts 10:34-35; Acts 10:15; Acts 11:17; Acts 10:28

It takes a vision repeated three times, an angel, the Spirit speaking out loud, and a houseful of Gentiles filled with God before the apostle Peter will finally admit a truth he should have known all along. The hardest wall to tear down is never the one between us and our enemies. It is the one we built ourselves and called holy.

**The Two Men God Was Already Moving**
Luke tells this story from both ends at once, so we can watch God close a gap from both sides. In Caesarea there is Cornelius — a Roman centurion, a Gentile, an officer of the army occupying the land, and yet a man who fears God with all his household, gives alms generously, and prays continually. An angel of God appears to him and tells him his prayers have risen as a memorial before God, and to send to Joppa for a man named Peter. And in Joppa, at the same hour, Peter goes up on a roof to pray and becomes hungry and falls into a trance, and he sees the heavens opened and a great sheet let down by its four corners, full of every kind of animal the law forbade him to eat, and he hears a voice: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat." Peter recoils hard — "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean" — and the voice corrects him: "What God has made clean, do not call common" (Acts 10:13-15). Three times, so the lesson cannot be waved off as a strange hungry dream. The vision is about food on its surface. It is about people underneath. While Peter sits there perplexed, wondering what it could mean, the men sent by Cornelius arrive at the gate below, and the Spirit tells him plainly: go with them, making no distinction. God has been working both ends of this toward each other all along, and the whole elaborate orchestration aims at one wall — the wall between Jew and Gentile, clean and unclean, us and them, the oldest and most sacred division Peter knew.

**The Confession Peter Is Forced To Make**
When Peter enters the centurion's house — already a scandal, an act that violated everything he had been taught, for as he says, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation" (Acts 10:28) — he says the line the whole vision had been driving him toward. "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him" (Acts 10:34-35). No partiality. The God who chose Israel was never the God of Israel only; he was always the God of the whole earth, who chose one nation to bless all of them. And as Peter is still in the middle of his sermon — preaching Christ crucified and raised, ordained by God to judge the living and the dead, the one to whom all the prophets bear witness, offering forgiveness of sins through his name — the Spirit cuts in before the altar call. "While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles" (Acts 10:44-45). The same Spirit, the same Pentecost, the same pouring out — now on the uncircumcised, while they are still uncircumcised. God did not wait for them to be made Jews first, did not require them to take on the law before he would take them in. He poured himself out on them as Gentiles, mid-sermon, before anyone could set the terms. Peter can only ask, "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" (Acts 10:47). God had already decided the matter. Peter was simply running to catch up with what God had done.

**The Argument That Ends With Praise**
The Jerusalem church does not throw a celebration when the news reaches them. They criticize him. "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them" (Acts 11:3). Eating with them — sharing a table, the most intimate sign of acceptance — is the offense. Peter does not argue theology or pull rank as the leading apostle. He simply tells them what God did, step by step, the vision and the sheet and the voice and the Spirit falling, and he ends with the question that ends the whole debate: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?" (Acts 11:17). And the room falls silent. And then the silence breaks into worship: "When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, 'Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life'" (Acts 11:18). Here is where I have to step into the indictment, because I keep a quiet list of the kinds of people the gospel is really for, and the list looks suspiciously like me and the people I already approve of. The early church had to be dragged into this truth by visions and an audible Spirit and an undeniable Pentecost — the truth that God has no second class, no inner circle of the genuinely acceptable and no outer ring of the barely tolerated, no first-rate Christians and no charity cases. The risen Christ tore the wall down from heaven precisely because the church would never have torn it down on its own. He poured his Spirit on the very people we would have kept standing outside the door, and the only thing left for any of us to do is to stop standing in his way.

God has no second class.

## Grace Alone, or No Gospel
*The council that guarded the door*

**Text:** Acts 15:1-35 · **Supporting:** Acts 15:11; Acts 15:10; Acts 15:1; Acts 15:19

The greatest threat the early church ever faced was not the persecutor at the gate or the executioner with the stones. It was the teacher inside the church who added one small word to the gospel. Not subtract — add. And the church had to decide, in a council that would shape every century after it, whether grace plus anything is still grace at all.

**The Word That Was Added**
The trouble comes dressed as devotion, which is how the worst trouble always comes. "But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, 'Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved'" (Acts 15:1). Notice the precise shape of the lie, because it is a shape that has outlived the first century by two thousand years. It does not deny Christ. It does not reject grace or attack the cross. It says: Christ, and. Faith, and circumcision. Grace, and the law of Moses. Believe in Jesus, yes, of course — and also keep these marks, carry these requirements, satisfy these conditions, or you cannot be saved. These men were not pagans infiltrating from outside; they were believers, members of the church, zealous for the Scriptures, sincere in their conviction that the old covenant signs still mattered to God. And that is exactly what made them so dangerous. The most lethal corruptions of the gospel have almost always come from inside the church, from earnest and devout people adding a requirement to faith out of genuine love for the tradition they inherited. Paul and Barnabas, who had just returned from watching God pour out his Spirit on uncircumcised Gentiles across Asia, have no small dissension and debate with them — Luke's dry understatement for what must have been a fierce fight — and because the question cannot be settled locally, the matter is sent up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and the elders, to be decided once and for all. The whole future shape of the church hangs on the answer they give.

**The Argument From What God Did**
After much debate, Peter stands and reaches all the way back to Cornelius, to the day the Spirit fell on the Gentiles in Caesarea. God himself bore witness to them, Peter says, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, "and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith" (Acts 15:9). By faith. Their hearts were cleansed by faith, not by the law, not by circumcision, not by adopting the customs of Moses. And then Peter names the real weight of what the circumcision party was trying to do. "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?" (Acts 15:10). The law was never a ladder anyone successfully climbed to God. It was a yoke no one in the whole history of Israel had ever managed to carry. To lay it now on the necks of the Gentiles is not to help them or complete them; it is to crush them under a weight Israel itself collapsed beneath. And then comes the verse that is the entire gospel compressed into a single breath: "But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will" (Acts 15:11). Hear the stunning direction of that sentence. Peter does not say the Gentiles will be saved the way we Jews are saved, by keeping the law. He says we Jews will be saved the way they are — by grace. Same door. Same Lord. Same grace. No special path for the religious, no head start for the circumcised, no second entrance for the people with the pedigree. James seals it with the witness of the prophets and delivers the council's verdict: "Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God" (Acts 15:19).

**The Gospel Worth Fighting For**
We are tempted to read this as a dusty old quarrel about an obsolete ceremony, a relic of the first century with nothing left to say to people who were never going to be circumcised anyway. That misreads it badly, and the misreading is dangerous, because the circumcision party is alive in every age and alive in me. The human heart is a machine built for adding conditions to grace; it does it automatically, without being taught. I am quietly, persistently sure that God accepts me more on the days I have prayed well, performed well, behaved well — that my standing before him rises and falls with my obedience, that the cross got me in the door but my effort keeps me in the room. That is Acts 15 dressed in modern clothes. It is the law smuggled back in through the side entrance, faith plus my record, grace plus my consistency, Christ plus my contribution, and the council understood what I am slow to feel: it is no gospel at all. A gospel of grace plus one small requirement is not a slightly weaker gospel; it is a different religion entirely, a religion of the self with Jesus added for support. So the council guarded the door with everything it had. They wrote a letter, sent it by trusted men, Judas and Silas, to ease the burden they had never authorized, and the Gentile churches "rejoiced because of its encouragement" (Acts 15:31). The risen Christ builds his church on grace alone, received through faith alone, and he will let his church endure persecution and scattering and prison and shipwreck — but he will not let it survive the quiet addition of a single condition to the cross. Because the very moment we add our one thing, we have stopped trusting him and started trusting the addition. And the addition has never saved anyone yet.

Grace alone, or no gospel.

## He Opens What We Cannot
*Three hearts the Lord broke open in Philippi*

**Text:** Acts 16:6-40 · **Supporting:** Acts 16:14; Acts 16:9; Acts 16:31; Acts 16:25

Paul tries to go one direction and the Spirit shuts the door. He tries another, and the Spirit shuts that one too. The mission to Philippi begins not with an open road but with God closing roads one after another, forbidding Paul to speak in Asia, refusing to let him enter Bithynia, until in the night a man from Macedonia stands before him in a vision and pleads, "Come over to Macedonia and help us" (Acts 16:9). The gospel does not arrive in Europe by Paul's careful planning. It arrives by Paul's plans being overruled until only one road is left open.

**The Heart God Opens**
In Philippi there is no synagogue, not even the ten Jewish men required to form one, so on the Sabbath Paul and his companions go outside the gate to the riverside, where they suppose there is a place of prayer, and they sit down and speak to the women who have gathered there. Among them is Lydia — a businesswoman from Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, which means a woman of means, a worshiper of God. She listens to what Paul says. And Luke tells us exactly how she comes to faith, in words that should stop every preacher cold, because the converting is not credited to Paul's argument or Lydia's openness. "The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul" (Acts 16:14). The Lord opened her heart. Lydia did not pry it open by an act of will. Paul did not lever it open by the force of his logic. The same risen Christ who opened the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf reaches into this woman and opens her heart to receive the word, and she and her household are baptized, and she presses her new brothers to stay in her home. This is the quiet center of the whole chapter, and it is the truth every evangelist eventually learns or breaks against. We preach, we reason, we plead, we lay the gospel out in order and beauty — and not one heart opens unless the Lord himself reaches in and opens it. I have stood in front of people with every argument arranged and watched nothing move, and I have watched the Lord open a heart I had privately given up on, and the difference was never my eloquence on the day. The seller of purple is the first convert on the continent of Europe, and she stands there as a monument to a truth that should make every preacher humble and every prayer desperate: he opens what we cannot.

**The Hearts We Would Not Choose**
Then the gospel reaches down past Lydia's respectable world to people it stepped over. A slave girl with a spirit of divination follows Paul through the streets, a girl owned by men who used her affliction to make money, and after many days of her crying out, Paul, annoyed, turns and casts the spirit out of her in the name of Jesus Christ. Her owners, who cared nothing for the girl and everything for their vanished profit, seize Paul and Silas and drag them before the magistrates, and the crowd joins in, and Paul and Silas are stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into the inner prison with their feet fastened in the stocks. And here is the third heart, in the strangest scene in the chapter. "About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them" (Acts 16:25). Beaten bloody, locked in the dark, feet in the stocks, backs torn open — and they sing. The prison becomes a sanctuary. Then a great earthquake shakes the foundations, the doors fly open, and every prisoner's bonds are loosed, and the jailer, waking to see the doors open and certain his prisoners have fled, draws his sword to kill himself, because Roman law would take his life for theirs. Paul stops him with a shout: "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here" (Acts 16:28). The jailer calls for lights, rushes in trembling, falls down before them, and asks the only question that finally matters: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" And the answer is the gospel stripped to the bone: "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household" (Acts 16:31). A wealthy businesswoman, a trafficked slave girl, a hardened Roman jailer — three people who shared nothing in this world but a Lord who opened the door for each of them.

**The Door No One Else Can Open**
Line the three of them up and see what they have in common, because it is everything that matters. Lydia has standing, money, a household, a trade. The slave girl has nothing at all, not even possession of her own body. The jailer has authority, a sword, a position in the empire. And not one of the three comes to Christ by anything they possess or anything they lack. Lydia's heart is opened by the Lord. The girl is set free by the name of Jesus. The jailer is saved by simple faith in the same Lord at midnight in the wreckage. The gospel does not climb the social ladder; it ignores the ladder entirely, treating the seller of purple and the slave and the jailer as the same kind of helpless case — and they are. And the means in every case is identical: the risen Christ opening what no human hand can open. I cannot open my own heart any more than Lydia could open hers. I could not argue myself into faith, could not perform my way through the door, could not earn the opening by being the right sort of person. He opened it. Paul preached and reasoned and sang, but the converting work belonged wholly to the Lord, in a businesswoman, a slave, and a jailer alike. The church the risen Christ builds is built entirely of people he reached down and opened, the riverside prayer meeting and the midnight prison cell all the same to him. He opens what we cannot. That is not a discouragement to a praying church. It is the only reason a praying church has any hope at all.

He opens what we cannot.

## Now He Commands Repentance Everywhere
*Paul among the philosophers of Athens*

**Text:** Acts 17:16-34 · **Supporting:** Acts 17:30; Acts 17:23; Acts 17:31; Acts 17:28

Paul walks into the most sophisticated city in the world, and the first thing Luke tells us is not what he thought but what he felt. Not impressed by the architecture. Not intimidated by the philosophy or the reputation of the place. "His spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16). Athens is a museum of the gods, a city so crowded with shrines that it was said to be easier to find a god there than a man, and Paul looks at all of it and grieves. The cultural capital of the ancient world is, to the apostle's eyes, a graveyard of worship aimed at no one who can hear it.

**The Altar to the Unknown God**
They bring Paul up to the Areopagus, to the council and the curious, to the Epicureans and the Stoics who spend their days, as Luke wryly notes, doing nothing but telling or hearing something new. They want to hear his strange new teaching. And Paul does not open the way we might expect. He does not flatter them by quoting their poets to win the room, and he does not condemn them by denouncing their idolatry to shame the room. He opens with something he actually saw walking their streets. "For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: 'To the unknown god.' What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you" (Acts 17:23). It is a brilliant and an honest move at once. The Athenians, covering every possible base, hedging against the danger of having neglected some deity they had never heard of, had built an altar to whatever god they might have missed — and Paul says, in effect, you are more right than you know. There is indeed a God you do not know, and I have come to tell you his name. He does not borrow their gods or baptize their pantheon. He confronts them with the one God they left off the list. He proclaims the Creator who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth who does not live in temples made by human hands, who is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. He made every nation from one man and determined their times and their boundaries, that they should seek him and perhaps feel their way toward him, though he is not far from any one of us. Even their own poets stumbled toward the truth: "In him we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:28). Paul grants the fragment of truth their best thinkers reached, and then turns it, showing them the living God their fragments were blindly groping after all along.

**The Turn From Ignorance to Command**
Then Paul makes the turn the whole speech was built toward, and it lands sharper than the Areopagus expected from a visiting lecturer. He has been generous about their ignorance; he has granted them their altar and their poets and their feeling after God in the dark. Now he ends the ignorance with a single word. "The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent" (Acts 17:30). Now. Something has changed in the history of the world. There was an age when the nations stumbled in the dark, groping after a God they could not name, and God in his patience bore with it, overlooked it, withheld his hand. That age is over. The Creator they had been worshiping without knowing has now stepped fully into the open, has made himself known, and the only fit response to a God who has revealed himself is no longer curiosity or speculation or one more altar. It is repentance. And why now? Why has the patience ended? "Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead" (Acts 17:31). There it is, dropped into the middle of the Areopagus like a stone into still water — the resurrection. A day is fixed on the calendar of heaven. A judge has been appointed to it. And the proof that this is no philosopher's clever theory, no Stoic abstraction, is that God raised the appointed judge from the dead. The Athenians wanted to add Paul's God to their collection, one more interesting altar among the hundreds, a fascinating idea to discuss over dinner. Paul will not be collected. He announces a Creator who commands, a day that is coming, and a risen man who will judge the living world. There is no neutral seat left in the Areopagus.

**The God Who Will Not Be Collected**
At the word resurrection, the room splits down the middle. "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this'" (Acts 17:32). Some sneered and walked out. A few wanted to hear more. And some believed — Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them. But I have to be careful preaching this, because Athens is not only out there in the secular university and the sophisticated city that wants to discuss God without bowing to him. Athens is in me. There is a part of me that wants exactly the God the Athenians wanted — a God I can examine, debate, file among my interests, add to my life alongside my other commitments, keep on a high shelf with my opinions where he is safe and I am in control. Paul preaches a God who flatly refuses that arrangement. He is not one altar among many. He is the Creator who now commands all people everywhere to repent, and that word everywhere leaves no exemption carved out for the educated, the cultured, the religiously curious, the pastor who would rather analyze him than fall down before him. The age of ignorance is over because the tomb is empty. And a risen judge does not request your consideration or apply for a place in your pantheon. He commands repentance — of the Athenian, of the skeptic, of the philosopher, and of the preacher who keeps trying to study a God who is standing up to judge.

Now he commands repentance everywhere.

## His Word Burns False Gods
*Ephesus, and a gospel that does not negotiate*

**Text:** Acts 19:1-41 · **Supporting:** Acts 19:20; Acts 19:19; Acts 19:26; Acts 19:27

The gospel comes to Ephesus and something catches fire — first a city, then a stack of books, then a riot in the theater. Ephesus was a center of magic and the proud home of the great temple of Artemis, one of the wonders of the ancient world, and into that whole economy of idols and spells Paul preaches the word of the Lord for two years. What follows is not peaceful coexistence. The word does not quietly move in beside the gods of Ephesus and take a room. It moves against them.

**The Books That Burned**
For two years Paul reasons daily in the hall of Tyrannus, and Luke says all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord. God does extraordinary miracles by Paul's hands. And then a telling thing happens: some itinerant Jewish exorcists, the seven sons of a man named Sceva, try to use the name of Jesus as a magic formula, commanding evil spirits by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims — and the evil spirit answers, "Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?" and the man with the spirit overpowers all of them so that they flee naked and wounded. The name of Jesus is not a technique anyone can pick up and wield. It belongs to those who belong to him. Fear falls on the whole city, Jew and Greek alike, and the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified. And then comes the scene that shows you what real repentance costs in a place like Ephesus. "And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver" (Acts 19:19). They did not sell the books to recover their investment. They did not quietly keep them in a drawer for reference, just in case. They burned them — a fortune in occult texts and incantations turned to ash in public, in front of everyone, because you cannot serve the risen Christ and keep your old gods stored safely away in case he should ever disappoint you. The conversion was not an addition to their existing religious life. It was a bonfire of everything that competed with him. And Luke gives the result of the whole episode as a single ringing verdict: "So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily" (Acts 19:20). The word grew as the idols burned. The two things are not separate. They are the same event seen from two sides.

**The Riot That Confessed the Truth**
The clearest testimony to the power of the gospel in Ephesus comes, strangely and wonderfully, from its enemy. A silversmith named Demetrius, who makes silver shrines of Artemis and brings no little business to the craftsmen of the city, gathers the workmen of that trade and tells them the truth about the gospel more honestly than many believers ever manage to. "Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods" (Acts 19:25-26). Listen to what the enemy openly admits to his own trade guild. The gospel is turning people away from idols, not by ones and twos but by the great many, not only in Ephesus but across the whole province. And then Demetrius names what he is actually afraid of, and it is worth weighing the order in which he names it. "There is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing" (Acts 19:27). The trade comes first; the goddess comes second. He dresses the whole thing up as zeal for Artemis, but the engine driving the riot is the threatened income. The city erupts, dragging Paul's companions into the theater, and for two solid hours the crowd shouts with one voice, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians," most of them not even knowing why they have come together. But the riot itself is the confession. They riot because the gospel works. A god who is genuinely nothing does not need a mob to defend him; the very fury, the very panic in the streets, proves that the word has touched something real and put it in mortal danger. The gospel did not flatter the culture or quietly add Jesus to the local pantheon as the newest option. It dethroned Artemis, and the whole city felt the throne shake.

**The Idol in My Drawer**
We like a gospel that adds to our lives and threatens nothing in them — a Jesus bolted neatly onto the existing arrangement, a new god placed politely on the shelf beside the old familiar ones, a savior who blesses my plans without ever disturbing my idols. Ephesus says plainly that this gospel does not exist anywhere outside our imaginations. The real word of the Lord burns books and empties temples and threatens the silversmiths' trade and starts riots, because it does not come to be added to a life; it comes to reign over one. And that forces a question I would rather avoid: what have I kept in the drawer? What have I decided Christ may have all of me except this one thing — the security I will not risk, the reputation I will not spend, the resentment I will not release, the appetite I have quietly exempted from his lordship and kept in reserve in case he disappoints me? The Ephesians counted the cost, found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver, and lit the match anyway. The risen Christ does not negotiate a settlement with the gods of the cities he enters or the gods of the hearts he saves. He grows as they burn. His word prevailed mightily in Ephesus not by accommodation but by conquest — quiet, total, costly — and the riot in the theater was only the false gods screaming as they fell.

His word burns false gods.

## The Chain Becomes the Pulpit
*Paul on trial, and a gospel that will not be jailed*

**Text:** Acts 21:27-26:32 · **Supporting:** Acts 26:8; Acts 26:22-23; Acts 23:11; Acts 26:29

Paul is seized in the temple at Jerusalem, dragged out, nearly beaten to death by a mob, rescued only by Roman soldiers, and the mission appears to be over. He will spend years in chains from here — interrogated, transferred from city to city, tried before crowd and council and two governors and a king. From the outside it looks like an interruption, the great missionary career grinding to a halt in a prison cell. From heaven it is a strategy. The chain that was meant to silence Paul becomes the very thing that sets him in front of the most powerful audiences of his entire life.

**The Defense That Became Testimony**
Watch what Paul does with every single trial, because it is the same move every time, and it tells you what kind of man the gospel makes. He is given the floor to defend himself against the charges, and every time he turns the legal defense into the proclamation of Christ. Before the screaming mob on the temple steps, given permission to speak, he tells the story of the Damascus road — how he too had once persecuted this Way to the death, and how the risen Lord stopped him. Before the Sanhedrin, before the governor Felix, before the governor Festus, before King Agrippa — again and again he tells it, the same story, the risen Christ who arrested him and called him and sent him to the Gentiles. Paul does not argue the legal technicalities of jurisdiction and procedure; he preaches Christ crucified and risen to whoever is compelled by the proceedings to sit and listen. Standing before King Agrippa, in chains, he puts the question that exposes the whole proceeding for what it really is: "Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead?" (Acts 26:8). The trial is supposed to be about Paul and his alleged crimes. Paul keeps making it about the resurrection. And he compresses his entire message into two verses that could have ended his life and instead defined it: "To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles" (Acts 26:22-23). The Christ must suffer. The Christ would rise. That is the hope Paul stands trial for, and he will not trade it for his freedom no matter how many courts he stands in.

**The Lord Who Stands by the Prisoner**
In the middle of these grinding years, on the night after the Sanhedrin trial dissolved into violence and Paul was hauled back to the barracks bruised and uncertain whether he would see morning, the risen Christ himself stands by him and tells him plainly why the chain exists. "The following night the Lord stood by him and said, 'Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome'" (Acts 23:11). The chain is not the end of the Rome mission Paul had dreamed of for years. The chain is precisely how the Rome mission is going to happen. Paul had longed to preach in Rome, the center of the world, and God is now taking him there — not as a free missionary buying his own passage, but as a prisoner of the empire, traveling at the empire's expense, under armed guard, with a guaranteed audience of governors and a king arranged along the way. The providence of it is staggering when you stop to see it. Every false accusation, every transfer, every maddening delay, every appeal is the risen Christ moving his witness step by step toward the heart of the world to testify before the great. The hope Paul preaches is not a hope that escapes suffering or routes around it. It is a hope that suffering cannot interrupt, cannot derail, cannot so much as slow down. The chain does not contradict the Lord's promise. The chain is how the Lord keeps it.

**The Witness Who Wanted the Court Converted**
The most revealing moment in all of it comes at the very end of the trial before Agrippa. The king, half-mocking and half-moved by Paul's testimony, says, "In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?" And Paul, the prisoner standing there in chains before a king on a throne, gives the answer that exposes the whole inversion of the scene: "Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains" (Acts 26:29). The prisoner pities the king. The accused longs for the conversion of his judges. There is no self-pity in Paul, no bitterness over the wasted years, no plea for sympathy, no demand for the justice he is owed — only the aching longing that everyone in the room, including the very men who hold the power to free him or kill him, would come to know the Christ he serves. And I have to measure myself honestly against that, because I treat my far smaller inconveniences as outrageous interruptions of the comfortable life I was apparently owed, and it would never once occur to me to want the people inconveniencing me to be saved. Paul saw no interruption in any of it. He saw a pulpit he could have reached no other way, an audience the gospel would never have gathered if he had stayed free. The risen Christ builds his church not only through the free and the strong and the unhindered, but through the bound and the accused and the falsely charged, taking the very worst the world's courts can do to his servant and turning it into the platform for his word. They put Paul in chains to stop his mouth. All they managed to do was change his audience.

The chain becomes the pulpit.

## Nothing Stops the Open Word
*Storm, shipwreck, and an open door at Rome*

**Text:** Acts 27:1-28:31 · **Supporting:** Acts 28:31; Acts 27:24; Acts 28:28; Acts 27:25

The book of Acts does not end with the triumph you would expect after thirty years of mission. No coronation, no great crowd, no temple, no public vindication of the man who carried the gospel across the world. It ends with a prisoner in a rented house at the heart of the empire, preaching to whoever comes, with no one able to stop him. Luke spends two long chapters getting Paul through a storm, a shipwreck, and a snakebite to reach that house — because the point of the entire book is hidden in the very last word of it, and the last word is unhindered.

**The God Who Keeps His Word Through the Storm**
The voyage to Rome falls apart almost from the start. Against Paul's warning, the ship sails on into the season of storms, and a violent wind called the northeaster sweeps down and seizes the vessel, and they are driven helplessly for days. They throw the cargo overboard with their own hands, then the ship's tackle, and for fourteen days they see neither sun nor stars, and at last, Luke says, all hope of being saved is abandoned. Two hundred and seventy-six souls are going to die in the sea. And in the very worst of it, when no one has eaten for days and the crew has given up, the prisoner stands up among them and tells them why they will live. "For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, and he said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you'" (Acts 27:23-24). You must stand before Caesar. The promise the risen Christ made to Paul that night in the Jerusalem barracks — that he would testify in Rome — is now the thing holding a doomed ship together in a storm that should have splintered it to driftwood. And Paul believes it without a hedge or a qualification: "So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told" (Acts 27:25). The ship runs aground and breaks apart in the pounding surf of Malta, and the soldiers move to kill the prisoners so none escape, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them, and every last one of the two hundred seventy-six reaches the shore alive, exactly as the angel had said. God steered Paul through a storm that swallowed the cargo and spared every passenger, because God had given his word and nothing in the whole raging sea could break it.

**The God Who Is Not Stopped by a Viper**
Washed up soaked and freezing on the beach of Malta, Paul does the humble thing — he gathers a bundle of sticks for the fire the islanders have kindled. And as he lays them on the flames, a viper, driven out by the sudden heat, fastens onto his hand and hangs there. The islanders watch and draw the obvious conclusion: this man escaped the sea, but Justice will not let him live; he must be a murderer the gods are finally catching up with. Paul simply shakes the snake off into the fire and suffers no harm at all, and the watching islanders, who expected him to swell up and drop dead, change their minds and decide he is a god. The sea could not drown him. The viper cannot poison him. God has said this man will reach Rome and stand before Caesar, and creation itself — wind, wave, rock, and serpent — cannot stop the word God means to bring to the capital. There is a pattern running straight across these two chapters, and the pattern is the entire point: every force that should by all rights have ended the mission — the storm, the shipwreck, the snake, the chains, the whole weight of the Roman Empire — bends around the promise of God. Paul is not a lucky man with an unusual run of survival. Paul is a carried man. The risen Christ who said you must stand before Caesar is sovereign over the wind and the rock and the viper and Rome itself, and Luke spends two unhurried chapters proving it before he will let the book come to rest.

**The Open Door That Does Not Close**
And then the ending, which is no ending at all, which Luke clearly designed to leave open on purpose. Paul reaches Rome at last, and though he is a prisoner under guard, he is allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guards him, and to receive all who come to him. He calls the local Jewish leaders together first and reasons with them about Jesus from morning till evening out of the Law and the Prophets, and when some believe and others will not, he turns, as he has turned so often, to the Gentiles: "Let it be known to you then that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen" (Acts 28:28). And then Luke closes the whole book — all the sermons, the prisons, the journeys, the councils, the miracles, the shipwreck — on this final note: "He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance" (Acts 28:30-31). Without hindrance. Unhindered. In the Greek it is the very last word of the book, and Luke leaves it deliberately ringing in the air. The book does not end at a wall. It ends at an open door, in the capital of the empire that thought it had Paul in custody. There is no period stamped on the mission here. The persecution that scattered the church only spread it. The chains that arrested Paul only carried the gospel to governors and kings. The storm could not drown the word and the empire could not jail it, and now the prisoner in Rome preaches the kingdom of God to all who come and no power on earth shuts his mouth. So I have to ask what I have quietly decided can stop this gospel in my life — what storm, what loss, what closed door, what wall I have looked at and concluded was the end of the story God was writing in me. Acts answers across two thousand years that there is no such wall. The risen Christ builds his church through prisons and storms and shipwrecks and open doors, and the book that records it refuses to close, because the open word he sends out into the world cannot be stopped by anything the world can do to it. The story is still being written. The door is still open.

Nothing stops the open word.
